lead: A short column under axial load is the simplest compression member: concrete and longitudinal steel shorten together and share the load until the concrete crushes. IS 456 turns this into one line of algebra, so the design is quick, but three details decide whether the answer is right: the concrete area must exclude the steel, the steel must stay between 0.8 % and 6 % of the section, and the ties or helix must follow the code. Most interior columns of an ordinary building are designed this way, and circular columns with a helix are used where extra strength and ductility are wanted.
prereq: You need the column types and the minimum eccentricity from Classification of columns; effective length and slenderness.

sections.h3: The axial load formula and when it applies

blocks.text: At failure the concrete in a short column is at its design compressive strength and the steel has yielded. IS 456 clause 39.3 takes the concrete stress as 0.4f<sub>ck</sub> and the steel stress as 0.67f<sub>y</sub>, values that already include a reduction for the minimum eccentricity:
P<sub>u</sub> = 0.4 f<sub>ck</sub> A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>sc</sub>,  with A<sub>c</sub> = A<sub>g</sub> − A<sub>sc</sub>
blocks.where: P<sub>u</sub> is the factored axial load in N; f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub> are the characteristic strengths of concrete and steel in N/mm²; A<sub>g</sub> is the gross area, A<sub>sc</sub> the area of longitudinal steel and A<sub>c</sub> the net concrete area, all in mm².

blocks.text: The formula is valid only when emin does not exceed 0.05 times the lateral dimension. If emin is larger, design the column for Pu with the moment Puemin as in Uniaxial and biaxial bending; interaction diagrams. Solving the formula for the steel gives Asc = (Pu − 0.4fckAg)/(0.67fy − 0.4fck).

sections.h3: Rules for longitudinal bars and ties (IS 456 clause 26.5.3)

items: Longitudinal steel: at least 0.8 % and at most 6 % of A<sub>g</sub> (4 % is a practical upper limit where bars are lapped).
At least 4 bars in a rectangular column and 6 in a circular column; bar diameter at least 12 mm; spacing along the perimeter not more than 300 mm.
Nominal cover to the longitudinal bars at least 40 mm (and not less than the bar diameter).
Tie diameter: not less than one quarter of the largest longitudinal bar, and not less than 6 mm.
Tie pitch: not more than the least of (i) the least lateral dimension, (ii) 16 times the smallest longitudinal bar diameter and (iii) 300 mm.
Every corner bar sits in a tie corner. A bar more than 75 mm from a restrained bar needs its own link, so the middle bar of a face gets an extra link.

blocks.text: Design steps: (1) write P<sub>u</sub>, f<sub>ck</sub>, f<sub>y</sub> and A<sub>g</sub>; (2) check that the column is short and e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05D; (3) find A<sub>sc</sub> from the formula and raise it to 0.8 % if smaller; (4) choose bars and check the capacity with the bars provided; (5) choose the ties.

A closely spaced helix confines the concrete core. When the core is fully confined the column keeps carrying load after the cover spalls. IS 456 clause 39.4 allows 1.05 times the tied-column strength if the helix is heavy enough:

blocks.where: V<sub>helix</sub> and V<sub>core</sub> are the volumes of helix steel and of core concrete per unit height; A<sub>k</sub> = πD<sub>k</sub>²/4 is the core area, D<sub>k</sub> being the core diameter measured to the outside of the helix.

blocks.text: The helix pitch must be not more than 75 mm and not more than D<sub>k</sub>/6, and not less than 25 mm or 3 times the helix bar diameter. A circular column with ordinary circular ties is designed like a tied column, without the factor 1.05.

examples.question: Design a braced short tied column of 400 mm × 400 mm, unsupported length 3.0 m, for a factored axial load of 2000 kN. Use M20 concrete and Fe415 steel.
steps: Slenderness: even with K = 1, 3000/400 = 7.5 < 12, so the column is short. e<sub>min</sub> = 3000/500 + 400/30 = 6.0 + 13.3 = 19.3 mm → 20 mm (floor). 0.05D = 0.05 × 400 = 20 mm, so e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05D and the axial formula applies.
Try 8 bars of 20 mm: 2513 mm², less than 2666; capacity 1958.7 kN < 2000 kN, not enough. Use 6 bars of 25 mm: A<sub>sc</sub> = 6 × 490.9 = 2945 mm² (1.84 %), 3 bars on each of two opposite faces.

Ties: diameter ≥ max(25/4 = 6.25 mm, 6 mm), so use 8 mm. Pitch ≤ least of 400 mm, 16 × 25 = 400 mm and 300 mm, so 300 mm. Each middle bar is about 140 mm from the corner bars (more than 75 mm), so it gets an extra 8 mm link.
examples.answer: 6 bars of 25 mm (2945 mm², 1.84 %) with 8 mm ties at 300 mm c/c and a link on each middle bar; capacity 2075 kN against 2000 kN.

examples.question: A circular column of 400 mm diameter with a helix carries a factored axial load of 1800 kN. Use M25 concrete, Fe415 steel, 40 mm clear cover to the helix and an 8 mm helix. Design the longitudinal steel and the helix pitch.
steps: A<sub>g</sub> = π × 400²/4 = 125664 mm². With the helix, P<sub>u</sub> = 1.05(0.4f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub>), so the tied strength needed is 1800/1.05 = 1714.3 kN.
Provide 6 bars of 20 mm (the minimum number for a circular column): 1885 mm² (1.50 %). Capacity = 1.05 × (10 × 123779 + 278.05 × 1885) = 1850.0 kN ≥ 1800 kN.
Helix volume per turn: 50.27 × π × (320 − 8) = 49269 mm³ (8 mm bar on a centre-line diameter of 312 mm). For pitch s, 49269/(80425 s) ≥ 0.01220 gives s ≤ 50.2 mm.
examples.answer: 6 bars of 20 mm with an 8 mm helix at 50 mm pitch; capacity 1850 kN.

traps: Using A<sub>g</sub> for the concrete term. That counts the concrete displaced by the bars and gives less steel than needed.
Using the axial formula when e<sub>min</sub> > 0.05D (for example a 300 mm side with e<sub>min</sub> = 20 mm). Such a column must be checked for P<sub>u</sub> with P<sub>u</sub>e<sub>min</sub>.
Quoting a fourth limit "48 × tie diameter" for the tie pitch. IS 456:2000 gives only three: least lateral dimension, 16 × smallest bar and 300 mm.
Taking the tie diameter from the smallest bar. It is one quarter of the largest bar, and never below 6 mm.
Applying the factor 1.05 to a circular column with plain ties, or measuring the core diameter to the centre of the helix instead of its outside.

quiz.q: Write the IS 456 axial load formula for a short tied column and state when it may be used.
quiz.a: P<sub>u</sub> = 0.4f<sub>ck</sub>A<sub>c</sub> + 0.67f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>sc</sub>, A<sub>c</sub> = A<sub>g</sub> − A<sub>sc</sub>; only when e<sub>min</sub> ≤ 0.05 × the lateral dimension.

quiz.q: State the three limits on the pitch of lateral ties.
quiz.a: Least lateral dimension of the column; 16 times the smallest longitudinal bar diameter; 300 mm. The least of the three governs.

quiz.q: Why does a helically reinforced column get 5 % more strength than a tied column?
quiz.a: The closely spaced helix confines the core, so after the cover spalls the core carries load at a higher stress and the column fails slowly. The code credits this with the factor 1.05 when the helix ratio meets 0.36(A<sub>g</sub>/A<sub>k</sub> − 1)f<sub>ck</sub>/f<sub>y</sub>.

quiz.q: A 450 mm × 450 mm braced short column, 3.2 m long, carries P<sub>u</sub> = 2400 kN (M20, Fe415). Find the longitudinal steel.
quiz.a: e<sub>min</sub> = 3200/500 + 450/30 = 21.4 mm ≤ 0.05 × 450 = 22.5 mm, so the axial formula applies. A<sub>sc</sub> = (2 400 000 − 0.4 × 20 × 202 500)/270.05 = 2888 mm² (minimum 1620 mm²). Provide 4 bars of 25 mm + 4 bars of 20 mm = 3220 mm² (1.59 %).

quiz.q: Design ties for a 350 mm × 500 mm column with 6 bars of 25 mm.
quiz.a: Diameter ≥ max(25/4 = 6.25, 6) → 8 mm. Pitch ≤ least of 350 mm, 16 × 25 = 400 mm and 300 mm → 300 mm. Use 8 mm ties at 300 mm c/c, with a link on any bar more than 75 mm from a tied corner.

quiz.q: For the 400 mm circular column of the second worked example, the pitch is changed to 60 mm. Is the column still a helically reinforced column?
quiz.a: Ratio = 49269/(80425 × 60) = 0.01021 < 0.01220. The helix is too light, so the factor 1.05 cannot be used; the capacity falls to 1762 kN, below 1800 kN.

beyond: Not for the exam. Weak columns are often strengthened with steel jackets or fibre-reinforced polymer wraps, which rely on the same confinement idea as the helix. Search for "FRP column confinement".
